w: Phase I is the non-surgical first step every gum patient gets, whatever their stage. These notes combine the 2026 slide deck with the recorded class. Dr. Kaur explained that D2 goes a step past D1. Instead of basics, it covers treatment: when it works, when it doesn't, and what the options are, so you're ready for clinic next year. She spent class on the exam and the reasons behind treatment, and saved the instrument details for the upcoming PCD (hands-on) sessions. What's on the midterm (Dr. Kaur's email after class): instruments, ultrasonic scalers and polishing won't be tested. Study the class discussion and the slides up to failure of therapy. In these notes, that's everything down to the section on the re-evaluation and when treatment "fails." The sections after it are marked. Flagged in class: about the diagram showing how bacteria and the body's immune response move a patient from health to gingivitis to periodontitis, she said "has anybody been counting? That's going to be on the quiz." Know what starts the disease, what makes it worse, and which one a deep cleaning actually treats. Start from the diagnosis Every patient fits one of three big groups: healthy gums, gingivitis (gum inflammation only) or periodontitis (gum disease that has destroyed bone). Healthy gums and gingivitis can each happen on a full-height set of supporting tissues (intact periodontium) or on one that has already lost some height (reduced periodontium). Periodontitis can't happen on an intact periodontium, because bone loss is what makes it periodontitis. You can't tell the three apart just by looking at a photo or into the mouth. You need the full gum chart (pocket depths, recession, attachment loss, furcations, loose teeth, how the gums look) plus the X-rays. The exam: plaque and gum health A full gum exam checks home hygiene (plaque score), gum health, pocket depths, attachment, furcations, the gum-to-cheek-lining border, loose teeth, the bite, and X-rays. It always starts with plaque, because plaque is the main cause of gum disease. There are two ways to record it. You can slide the probe about 1 mm into the gum crevice (this isn't measuring the pocket) and score each spot 1 if plaque comes out on the probe and 0 if not. Or the patient chews a disclosing tablet (lavender or pink in the clinic), rinses briefly, and you wipe the extra dye off the cheeks and tongue, show them in a mirror and record the score. Both methods only record whether plaque is there or not, not how much. Measuring amount (near the gum only, half the tooth, the whole tooth) at every spot would take far too long. Gum health is judged by color (redness), texture (swelling), bleeding when probed (BOP) and a gingival index. Bleeding is recorded while you probe: 1 if the spot bleeds, 0 if not. Late bleeding counts. After you've moved on a couple of teeth or to the next quarter of the mouth, look back. Any earlier spot that has started bleeding still gets a 1. Not every periodontitis patient looks the same, because other factors change how the gums appear. Smoking hides inflammation: nicotine squeezes blood vessels, so the gums often look bluish-gray instead of puffy and bleeding. Diabetes makes inflammation look worse. Gum overgrowth caused by a medication tells you something in the medical history is adding to the picture. The class example was a patient with high blood pressure taking amlodipine (a calcium channel blocker). The gums were bulging, mostly between the teeth, and more on the cheek/lip side than the tongue/palate side. The four patients shown, all from the student clinic, all had periodontitis. Their gums looked quite different, including one with uncontrolled diabetes who was also on a calcium channel blocker. Probing, recession and CAL Probing records six spots per tooth (DB, B, MB, DL, L, ML), taking the deepest reading at each. Probing depth runs from the gum edge to the bottom of the pocket. Recession runs from the CEJ (the line where enamel meets root) to the gum edge. Clinical attachment level runs from the CEJ to the bottom of the pocket, so CAL = probing depth + recession. The deck's pair: a 7 mm pocket with no recession and a 2 mm pocket with 5 mm of recession both have a CAL of 7 mm. Her big point: in healthy gums, pocket depth is not the same as attachment level. Healthy gum sits a little above the CEJ and covers it. Recession is positive when the gum has pulled back and you can see the CEJ. It's negative when the gum edge sits above the CEJ: −1, −2, −3, or even more with medication-caused overgrowth. Add it with its sign. A 5 mm pocket with −3 mm recession is a CAL of 2 mm. Skip the recession and the same spot reads 5 mm, which would point to Stage 3 or 4 disease even if the X-rays show only about 20% bone loss. Pocket depths, attachment levels and X-rays should all tell the same story. The same mistake happens in Salud, the charting software. If you leave recession blank, or type 0 without checking whether it's really positive or negative, Salud makes CAL equal to pocket depth. A blank over-diagnoses disease, and an automatic zero is inaccurate too. Enter the real number with its sign and Salud does the math correctly. To measure negative recession you have to feel the CEJ, since you can't see it. Slide the probe to the bottom of the pocket, then slowly pull it out until you feel the rough CEJ. The millimeters still under the gum at that point are the negative recession, which you subtract from the pocket depth. It's harder with lots of inflammation or overgrowth (both caused by disease), with altered passive eruption (a normal variation), and with tartar or filling edges that can feel like a CEJ. On eruption: as a tooth comes in, active eruption is the tooth moving up to meet the opposite tooth, and passive eruption is the gum moving down to settle at the CEJ. In altered passive eruption the gum never moves down, so its edge stays well above the CEJ. Getting good at this takes practice. The probe is the most important exam tool. Press lightly, feel for the springy stop, and keep it parallel to the tooth. Between teeth, don't stop at the corner of the tooth (the line angle). Go past it and under the contact point (front teeth) or contact area (back teeth), tilting slightly toward the spot just below the contact. When you can't probe yet: debridement Debridement isn't a treatment. You never do it to treat disease, and it should never be combined with scaling and root planing (deep cleaning). The only reason to do it is tartar so heavy that you can't see or feel the gum edge, so you can't take any measurements. There's only a full-mouth debridement code, no half-mouth or single-area version. It's meant for tartar so widespread it covers even the chewing surfaces, which is rare. Insurance won't pay for debridement and a gum exam at the same visit: if you couldn't measure before, the gums won't be ready right after. So in private practice the patient usually comes back in about two weeks for the full chart. School is more flexible. The first gum charting is free, so after clearing a patch of heavy tartar you can do the full chart at the same visit if the gums look okay. Check with your faculty, who may want to let the gums settle for two weeks. Combining saves the patient a trip. In private practice you can also choose not to charge for a small debridement, though a packed hygiene schedule is often a reason to split visits anyway. Furcations: named classes, not millimeters A furcation is where a tooth's roots split. It's checked with the Nabers probe, which is curved with light and dark bands every 3 mm, alongside X-rays. Even so, the grading used here is the Glickman classification, which is based on what you feel, not a millimeter count. Class I does not mean "3 mm or less." Class I, just starting. The probe barely catches. Usually no treatment. Easy to keep stable as long as the attachment and pocket don't get worse. Class II, a dead end. The probe goes clearly into the furcation, but bone still stands on the far side (probe from the cheek side and the palate/tongue-side bone is still there). Because it's a contained pocket with depth, it's the class best suited to regrowing bone (regeneration). Class III, all the way through. The hardest to treat. Nothing contains it, so it can't regrow. Class IV. A Class III where the gum has also pulled back (naturally or by surgery), so you can see through it. The patient can clean it with little brushes or a water flosser, but the exposed roots risk sensitivity and root cavities. A cavity in a furcation makes the tooth hopeless (it will need to come out), so watch these teeth closely at every maintenance visit. Her cases: an upper molar (#3) with furcation involvement was the only back support for a bridge. Instead of pulling it, they turned the Class III into a Class IV (cleaned it and moved the gum down so the patient could reach it). That patient is still doing well. Another patient given the same treatment got a large cavity under the roof of the furcation. Gum border, loose teeth and the bite The gum border check asks how much firm (keratinized) gum the patient has. Measure its width directly, or use the rolling technique: roll the loose cheek lining up toward the teeth until it stops at the mucogingival junction (where firm gum begins). This matters around implants as well as teeth. Looseness is checked with two rigid, blunt instrument handles, one on each side of the tooth, and graded on the Miller scale: 0 is normal, 1 is a little more than normal (under 1 mm), 2 is moderately more (between 1 and 2 mm), and 3 is severe side-to-side movement plus the tooth can be pushed down into its socket. A tooth that pushes down into its socket is ready to come out. That's looseness at rest. Fremitus is looseness while the teeth work. Put a finger on the root while the patient taps their teeth together and feel for vibration. It can go up-and-down and/or side-to-side, and you usually feel it rather than see it. If you feel fremitus, find out why that tooth is taking so much force. In the class example, missing back teeth meant the premolars were doing the molars' job. The gum chart has no box for bite findings, so put them in the notes section: wear patterns, acid erosion, vertical bone defects and whether they link to a bite problem, and grinding or clenching. This matters because a loose tooth isn't always just gum disease. It can be too much biting force on a tooth that has already lost support, from missing back teeth, grinding, or overjet and overbite. Treating a 5 mm pocket won't fix grade 2 looseness unless the bite is fixed too. The deck's list of bite warning signs: grinding or clenching habits, loose teeth, fremitus, drifting teeth, open contacts, unusual wear and wear facets, possible jaw-joint pain, vertical bone defects and a widened ligament space on X-ray. X-rays, before you touch the patient Before you take any measurements, X-rays show whether there's bone loss, whether it's in a few spots or all over, and its pattern (flat, vertical, or both). They also show tipped teeth, fused roots, roots too close together (important for surgery and deep cleaning), tartar, how close the sinus is, and an infection at a root tip (#7 in the class X-ray). Seeing tartar on an X-ray should make you "a little bit of both" sad and excited. Sad the patient got to that point, excited because now you know the cause and it's something you can remove. Once tartar has formed the patient can't brush it off, so your job matters even more. Her tip: when you start a deep cleaning (or even a regular cleaning), don't open the chart to hunt for deep pockets. Your instrument will find the pocket, and the bottom of the pocket is where you stop. Open the X-rays instead (take screenshots, since Salud logs you out). Then roughness on #14-15 matches tartar you already saw, and pus or a draining spot on #7 matches the root-tip infection. Look at the X-rays before you start measuring. Why Phase I works: bacteria start it, the body drives it Plaque bacteria start the disease. The body's immune response is what makes it get worse. In health the immune system handles the bacteria quickly and the bacteria aren't very harmful, so disease never shows. In gingivitis the bacteria change and the attack gets stronger. The body still wins, but it takes longer: more immune cells (T cells and B cells) join the first responders (neutrophils), and you see inflammation for days to a couple of weeks. Not everyone moves from reversible inflammation to permanent damage. Those who do have an immune system that overreacts and releases inflammatory signals (cytokines). Environment, genes, habits and gene-switching (epigenetic) factors add to the risk. The result is lost attachment, lost bone, and damage to the ligament, root surface and bone around the tooth. Deep cleaning targets the bacteria, yet bacteria cause only about 25% of the damage. About 75% comes from the body's own inflammatory signals and bone-dissolving cells (osteoclasts). Bacteria bring toxins (endotoxin, also called lipopolysaccharide), not osteoclasts. Removing the bacteria calms the body's response. Some patients still have disease after good home care and the best cleaning or surgery. For them, drugs can calm the body's response directly. That's host modulation, or "periodontal medicine," which Dr. Litz covers later. Bacteria coat tartar and live inside its tiny channels, and tartar and plaque also act as irritants the body reacts to. The goals of removing them: less inflammation, a shift in the pocket bacteria from the harmful gram-negative kind toward gram-positive (healthy mouths still have bacteria, just friendlier ones), and stopping the disease from getting worse. Deep cleaning doesn't undo the damage. Lost bone and attachment stay lost, which is why periodontitis is called irreversible. And getting rid of pockets is not the reason for deep cleaning, even though pockets do shrink. A pocket is a space the patient can't clean, full of more harmful bacteria. Phase I changes that environment. How pockets shrink, and why you check at 4-6 weeks Two things make a pocket shallower. At the top: inflamed gum is swollen with extra cells and fluid. As it calms down the gum shrinks, which you measure as more recession. At the bottom: disease had broken both the thin seal of gum cells against the tooth (the junctional epithelium, which is why the probe sank deeper) and the fibers holding the gum to the root. After cleaning, both reattach to the clean root. You measure in two dimensions, but the disease is three-dimensional. The healing timeline: the gum seal (junctional epithelium) takes 7-10 days, the fiber reattachment takes 4-6 weeks, and the fibers mature and line up over 3-6 months. That's why the patient comes back at 4-6 weeks. You see the full result by then, and research shows waiting longer doesn't shrink the pocket any further. The deck says it a bit differently: pockets shrink most in the first 4 weeks, the seal between gum and tooth re-forms in 2-4 weeks, and healing can keep going for 9-12 months. Know both. The deck's "a 6 mm pocket might become 5 or 4.5" numbers are just for a sense of scale. She said you don't need to memorize them. The words (and the billing codes) Scaling removes soft and hard buildup from teeth, roots and any bridges or dentures, both above and below the gum. If you're asked whether scaling is above or below the gum, the answer is both. Root planing stays below the gum and only works on roots. It smooths away rough, tartar-packed or contaminated root surface until there are no ridges, rough spots or catches. In practice you do both together. A prophylaxis ("prophy") is a preventive cleaning, not a treatment, for someone who has never had periodontitis (healthy gums or gingivitis). Tartar a little below the gum doesn't mean periodontitis: everyone has a shallow crevice, and tartar 1-2 mm down is removed as part of the prophy. Periodontal maintenance is ongoing support for someone already treated for periodontitis, to keep the disease from coming back, with their home care checked every visit. The two terms don't mean the same thing. A maintenance patient with mostly 1-3 mm pockets, a few leftover 4s and one 5 can stay on maintenance if their hygiene is good, those spots don't bleed, the gums look healthy and the X-rays show no new bone loss. Deep cleaning just the few leftover deep pockets is officially part of maintenance. Scaling in the presence of gingival inflammation (D4346) sits between a prophy and a deep cleaning. It's for someone never diagnosed with periodontitis, with no bone loss, but with heavy, widespread gum inflammation caused by plaque and tartar, so a simple prophy doesn't cover the work. At school it's done with perio faculty or a resident and gets a Phase I re-evaluation. The class case was a young patient (20s to early 30s) with a bridge of tartar on the tongue side of the teeth. What looked like bone loss around the premolars and front of the molars came from premolars pulled for braces and the tipping that followed, not from periodontitis. Diagnosis: widespread gum inflammation on a reduced periodontium in a patient without periodontitis (the deck calls it gingivitis on a reduced periodontium), treated with D4346. That patient had debridement, charting and treatment all in one visit. Full-mouth debridement (D4355) is a rough clean-out so the proper exam can happen at a later visit. What the evidence says about how to do it Splitting the deep cleaning into several visits doesn't really help: tartar left behind after several visits stays for the same reasons it stays after one (Anderson 1996). Hand instruments and ultrasonic (powered) scalers work about the same for shrinking pockets and regaining attachment, and adding under-the-gum rinsing with chlorhexidine, saline or peroxide adds nothing. In pockets 5 mm or deeper, the root isn't fully cleaned about 65% of the time (Greenstein 2000). What makes it hard, as she taught it: deeper pockets are harder to reach, though a 5 mm pocket doesn't mean tartar gets left every time. Deep cleaning is done blind: you work by feel. Some bacteria swim into the gum lining, while cleaning only reaches the pocket (and it doesn't reliably wipe out A. actinomycetemcomitans). Fillings and crowns with overhanging, below-the-gum, open or rough edges collect plaque and are hard to clean around. Furcations and the natural grooves and dips in roots block access. Trying hard for a smooth root can take off too much root surface (cementum) and make teeth sensitive. And results depend on the patient's home care and the clinician's skill, which improves with practice. The re-evaluation, and when it "fails" Check back at 4-6 weeks: plaque scores, signs of inflammation, bleeding, pocket depths, recession, attachment, looseness, furcations and pus. This is where the decision about surgery is made. If there's still inflammation and the numbers haven't improved, check whether leftover tartar is the reason. You'll often feel it with the probe while re-measuring. If so, remove it (no charge) and re-check in two weeks. If you already got all the tartar the first time, more rounds of deep cleaning won't help. What helps is better home care. "Failure of therapy" is a harsh phrase, because so much is out of your control. The body's response affects healing as well as disease. A smoker or someone with uncontrolled diabetes may not get the same short- or long-term result from your best cleaning. The deck's approach when Phase I doesn't work: look at how the gums responded, what tartar is left, the health history and risk factors, and maybe a plaque culture. Then choose antibiotics or antimicrobials, host-modulation drugs, a repeat cleaning, another re-evaluation, or Phase II, which is surgery to get rid of pockets. The instruments (not on the midterm) Dr. Kaur's email says instruments, ultrasonic scalers and polishing won't be on the midterm. In the slides they come after failure of therapy. The email is only about the midterm, so this can still show up on the final and in the hands-on instrument check. She kept instruments light on purpose. They get covered in detail in the upcoming PCD sessions, and you don't need the numbers yet, though you will later. For now, your daily kit has three groups. The exam tools are the mirror, the gum probe, the Nabers probe for furcations, and a gum explorer. This isn't the cavity explorer. You use it after cleaning to check that roots feel smooth with no catches. Then come scalers and curettes. Every instrument has a handle, a shank (the neck) and a blade. Scalers are mostly for above the gum. They reach only a little way under it (the deck says 1-2 mm; in class she said about 2-3, noting sources vary). Their strokes are short, strong and fast. Curettes go deep into the pocket with longer, slightly lighter strokes that take more time, though stubborn tartar can still need real pressure. The key difference is the blade. A scaler cuts on both sides. A Gracey curette cuts on one side only, so below the gum the side facing the gum can't cut it. Almost every curette in your kit is a Gracey, marked SG, each shaped for one area and cutting on one side. The one SC instrument is the universal curette, which, like a scaler, cuts on both sides. The clinic has piezoelectric ultrasonic (vibrating) scalers along with hand instruments. They work below the gum too, but they can't root plane, so they won't leave the root smooth. Use them together: ultrasonic to knock off the heavy tartar, then hand instruments, then the ultrasonic again so its water spray flushes out the pocket. From the deck, for later: gum hand instruments are mirrors, explorers, probes, scaling and root-planing tools, and polishing tools. The mirror lets you see indirectly, bounces light in, and holds the cheek or tongue back. The ODU 11/12 explorer is run over every surface of every tooth to feel for rough root. Its neck is shaped like the Gracey 11/12. Slide it in with the lower neck parallel to the tooth until you feel the slight resistance of the gum attachment, then stroke up-and-down and side-to-side with the side of the tip. The UNC-15 probe is 15 mm long. The exam kit is probe, explorer, Nabers probe, mirror and cotton pliers. A sickle scaler has a pointed tip, a triangle-shaped cross-section and two cutting edges, and shouldn't be used much on exposed root. Hook it under the ledge of tartar and pull with short, strong strokes using the lower third of the blade. The H6/7 (straight neck) is for front teeth and the cheek/tongue sides of molars. The S204SD9 (neck bent at a right angle) is for the spaces between back teeth. Both are held at about 80° to the root. A curette has a rounded tip and a half-moon cross-section and works above and below the gum. A universal curette (Columbia 13/14) has two cutting edges. An area-specific Gracey has one. Gracey curettes have a 70° blade angle, one cutting edge (the lower one), and a rounded back so they don't cut the gum. The lower neck should sit parallel to the tooth. Slide it in nearly flat (closed), then open it to 70-80° against the root to work. Which one goes where: 3/4 (or 1/2, 7/8) for all surfaces of front teeth (the demo slide adds premolars) and deep tartar. 11/12 for the mesial (front-facing) surfaces of back teeth plus the cheek/tongue sides of molars. 15/16 as another mesial tool for back teeth. 13/14 for the distal (back-facing) surfaces of back teeth. The 13/14 has more bends in its neck than the 11/12 and is pulled from root toward crown or from back toward front. Ultrasonic scalers come in two types. Magnetostrictive: electricity makes the nickel-iron metal stack in the insert change shape and vibrate in an oval-to-circular pattern, about 18,000-42,000 times a second, so every side of the tip can clean. Piezoelectric: electricity vibrates crystals in the handpiece, the tip moves back and forth in a line, and mainly its sides do the work. For implants, probes are marked in 3 mm bands (3-6-9-12 or 3-6-8-11), and the listed tools are front and back sickle scalers plus the Columbia 4R/4L. Technique (not on the midterm) Don't forget (the deck's own emphasis): modified pen grasp and a finger rest. A finger rest (fulcrum) steadies your hand. There are four: conventional (on the teeth right next to where you're working), cross-arch (on the other side of the same jaw), opposite-arch (on the other jaw), and finger-on-finger (on the index finger or thumb of your other hand). How you fit the instrument to the tooth depends on the gum (tough and fibrous vs. puffy and bleeding), how bad the disease is (how easily the gum moves aside, the space between teeth), and how stuck-on the tartar is. An exploratory stroke is light, with the tool fitted to the tooth, to map the pocket and find tartar. A working stroke uses a firm grip with pressure through the tip. Scaling strokes are short, overlapping, strong and controlled. Root-planing strokes are longer and lighter, like shaving. You check your work during the visit by feeling the root with an explorer, and at re-evaluation by how the gums respond: less redness, swelling and bleeding. The patient's home care weighs heavily on that result. The spots most often missed are the CEJ, furcation entrances, line angles (corners of the teeth), and hard-to-reach areas, especially the back surfaces of back teeth. To polish or not to polish (not on the midterm) For polishing: it removes stain that brushing and scaling leave behind, preps teeth for sealants, fluoride gels and varnishes, and patients like it. Against: 30 seconds with pumice can take off up to 4 µm of enamel, and that outer layer has the most fluoride. A coarse paste can leave the surface rougher than before. Steady pressure from a fast-spinning rubber cup can hurt and may heat the nerve. A rubber cup with pumice for 2 minutes can strip the thin lining inside the gum pocket completely, and pumice can get pushed under the gum. If you polish, use a low-abrasion paste on a slow handpiece with little heat, hold the cup at 90° to the tooth, and press lightly on and off. (Polishing comes from the deck. It wasn't covered in the recorded class.)
